Roman law for the first time distinguished breaches of contract from tortious acts. Prior to that, as in ancient Greece, non-performance was simply regarded as infringement. Various provisions of the Roman law have become the origin of modern contract law in Continental Europe, based on which the French Civil Code (Code Civil des Franςais 1804) and the German Civil Code (Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) were drafted. The French Civil Code established for the first time the principle of freedom of contract, which has become the core principle of modern contract law.

In England, the principles of modern contract law were well developed in common law courts in the early 19th century. The first important treatise expounding the English law of contract was arguably John Powell’s Essay upon the Law of Contracts and Agreements. The concept of freedom of contract, originating in the work of Adam Smith, was well summed up in the words of a judge in 1875 in the case of Printing and Numerical Registering Co. v. The three pieces of legislation on contract law were not intended to be a comprehensive set. They were enacted piecemeal to solve the immediate needs of the economic reform starting from 1979. They contained contradictory provisions, and the scope of each of them overlapped. In 1993, the drafting process of a new Contract Law started, which was intended to replace the three pieces of legislation. It is believed that the drafters of the new Contract Law, consisting of many legal academics this time, had made extensive reference to various sources, such as the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (PICC) (http://www.unidroit.org/english/principles/contracts/main.htm),the United Nations Convention on Contracts for International Sale of Goods (CISG) (http://www.uncitral.org/uncitral/en/uncitral_texts/sale_goods.html), the Principles of European Contract Law (PECL) (http://frontpage.cbs.dk/law/commission_on_european_contract_law/), the civil codes of France and Germany, and the English common law. It was passed on 15 March 1999, effective 1 October 1999, and was supplemented by the Interpretation on Several Issues Regarding the Application of the Contract Law (1) (http://www.sjzmbc.gov.cn/en/public/englishshow.jsp?id=20060904158511) issued by the Supreme People’s Court and some other judicial interpretations on technology contract and construction contract.

[exc_3af200c915ae90_9_v2] Chinese Contract Law — Chapter 1 General principles of contract law › Activity 1.1 › 5 (pages 8)
roles: introduction | topics: chinese-contract-law-history
teaches: Explains how merchant tribunals and lex mercatoria entered English and U.S. common law, then contrasts reputation-based enforcement in Western jurisdictions with the source's assessment of commercial dispute resolution in China.
scope: Historical comparative background, not a chronology of Chinese legislation. Claims that business ethics in China had yet to be cultivated, judgment enforcement was immature, and many disputes used non-legal means are the 2009 textbook's characterizations, not current findings.
In the US, merchants had tried to avoid the time-consuming court procedures for resolving commercial disputes until the end of the 18th century. Similar to the situation in England, the outcome of the competition between courts of law and merchants’ tribunals was that the customs of merchants were absorbed by judges and integrated into the common law.

The experience in Western jurisdictions shows that merchants’ concern about their goodwill and long-term reputation, rather than the effectiveness of the court system, is probably the biggest driving force behind the enforceability of contracts. In China, however, business ethics have yet to be cultivated. The deterrent force of peer pressure on contract breakers remains to be seen. Coupled with the immature system of the enforcement of court judgments, it is hardly surprising that many commercial disputes in China are resolved by non-legal means.

In the next section of the unit, you will find out more about the key milestones in the historical development of Chinese contract law.

[exc_3af200c915ae90_42_v2] Chinese Contract Law — “ › Case Study 1.3 › 18 (pages 21)
roles: exercise, worked_example | topics: chinese-contract-concept-and-scope | figures: fig_3af200c915ae90_216_v2
Scope not reviewed. Check the source's applicability before using it.
In Continental civil law jurisdictions such as Germany, Japan, France, Switzerland and Italy, the contract law is found within the civil code or the code of obligations. Contract law, tort law and the law of unjust enrichment are all regarded as part of the law of obligations.

At the time of writing, China’s civil code is still in the drafting stage. The General Principles of Civil Law and the Contract Law remain the sources of Chinese contract law. In addition, the Sino-foreign Equity Joint Venture Law and the Sino-Foreign Cooperative Joint Venture Law contain specific provisions on Sino-foreign joint venture contracts.

Administrative rules and regulations also constitute sources of the Chinese contract law. Furthermore, according to article 125 of the Contract Law, ‘transaction practices’ may also be the so urces of contract law.

title: Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law
content:
# Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law

*Based on the open textbook **Chinese Contract Law**, Chapter 1 (General principles of contract law), §1.2. A 2009 textbook: statements about "current" law reflect that period.*

## 1. Comparative background (why China's path matters)

- **Code of Hammurabi (c. 1792 BC):** 282 articles, of which 150 (over 53%) dealt with contractual relationships (sales, leases, adoption, marriage); fault liability, strict formalism, harsh enforcement.
- **Roman law:** first to distinguish breach of contract from tortious acts (before that, as in ancient Greece, non-performance was simply infringement). Its provisions became the origin of modern Continental contract law, underlying the **French Civil Code (1804)** and the **German Civil Code (BGB)**.
- **French Civil Code:** first codified the principle of **freedom of contract**, now the core principle of modern contract law.
- **England:** modern contract principles developed in common law courts in the early 19th century; freedom of contract (traced to Adam Smith) famously stated in *Printing and Numerical Registering Co. v. Sampson* (1875).

## 2. Imperial China (pre-1911)

- Whether civil law existed in Imperial China is **debatable**: Liang Chichao (梁啟超) and Wang Boqi (王伯琦) argued civil law (as opposed to criminal law) simply did not exist; Yang Honglie (楊鴻烈) held the opposite view.
- Beyond dispute: **no civil code ever existed** in Imperial China, though there was separate legislation on marriage and debt.

## 3. Late Qing: first draft civil code

- **1902:** Emperor Guang Xu formed a team to draft a civil code modelled on Continental European codes.
- Drafting ran **1908–1910**, producing the **Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (《大清民律草案》)** — the first civil code in China's history, though only in draft form.
- **Never enacted**: the Qing Dynasty was overthrown shortly thereafter.

## 4. Republican era: first enacted civil code

- **April 1927:** National Government established; **December 1928:** the Legislative Yuan took charge of drafting.
- **January 1929:** Drafting Committee of the Civil Code set up; compilation began February 1929.
- **26 December 1930:** the **Civil Law of the Republic of China (《中華民國民法》)** promulgated — the first enacted civil code in China's history, containing detailed contract law provisions.

## 5. People's Republic of China (post-1949)

- **1954:** drafting of a new civil code began; a draft was completed in **December 1956**, but enactment was derailed by the antirightist movements and the Cultural Revolution. Political unrest halted in 1978.
- Rather than revisit the old draft, China legislated on contracts **piecemeal** to serve the economic reform starting from 1979:
  - **Economic Contract Law (1981)**
  - **Foreign Economic Contract Law (1985)**
  - **Technology Contract Law (1987)**
- These three statutes were **not a comprehensive set**: they contained contradictory provisions and overlapping scopes.
- The **General Principles of Civil Law (GPCL)**, enacted in 1985 per the source, is **not a civil code** — only "general principles," like the introductory chapter of a civil code still in the drafting stage (as of the textbook's writing).

## 6. The 1999 Contract Law

- **1993:** drafting of a new Contract Law began, intended to replace the three 1980s statutes.
- Drafters (many legal academics) drew extensively on: the **UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (PICC)**, the **CISG**, the **Principles of European Contract Law (PECL)**, the French and German civil codes, and English common law.
- **Passed 15 March 1999; effective 1 October 1999.**
- Supplemented by the Supreme People's Court's *Interpretation on Several Issues Regarding the Application of the Contract Law (1)* and other judicial interpretations on technology and construction contracts.

## Key takeaways

1. China's contract law developed by **transplanting Continental (and, to a degree, common law) models**, first via the Qing draft and the 1930 Republican civil code.
2. PRC codification was repeatedly interrupted; contract rules arrived **piecemeal** in the 1980s before being unified in 1999.
3. The 1999 Contract Law is a product of **international harmonization sources** (PICC, CISG, PECL) as much as domestic tradition.

I created the study note **"Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law"** (id `mat_54a6fc6685baf5b3`), a concise, sectioned note built entirely from the *Chinese Contract Law* open textbook (Chapter 1, §1.2). It covers:

- **Imperial China** — the scholarly debate over whether civil law existed (Liang Chichao/Wang Boqi vs. Yang Honglie) and the absence of any civil code
- **Late Qing** — the Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (1908–1910), never enacted
- **Republican era** — the 1930 Civil Law of the Republic of China, the first enacted civil code with detailed contract provisions
- **PRC era** — the failed 1954–1956 codification, the three piecemeal 1980s contract statutes (Economic, Foreign Economic, Technology), and the GPCL
